..
Issued at 1026 PM MDT Wed Sep 23 2026

A shortwave trough is getting pinched by high pressure ridge 
trying to build back over the west, forming a Rex Block with a 
low over the Baja. This is introducing some drier air in from 
the northwest and across eastern Utah, resulting in clearing 
skies across the northwest portions of the CWA and shunting the 
deeper moisture plume further east. This moisture is currently 
being squeezed between the shortwave trough to our west and high
pressure to our east, with showers currently concentrated 
across southwest Colorado and up the central divide and areas 
east of the divide. These showers are fairly shallow with low 
tops but still producing light to moderate stratiform rainfall 
underneath across our southern mountains and valleys. Over the 
last 36 hours, precipitation totals across these areas range 
from 0.5 to 1.5 inches, with the higher amounts concentrated the
southern and eastern San Juans as well as San Juan River Basin 
and eastern portions of the Animas River Basin. This is 
providing a good soaking rain, which this area has been getting 
plenty of over the past couple weeks. Little instability and 
lack of forcing isn't quite resulting in the heavier rates or 
convection needed to cause flash flooding and the rivers have 
seen a little response, but nothing concerning at the moment. 
Winds have also been on the lighter side due to the cloud cover 
and more stratiform nature. However, as anticipated, 
thunderstorm activity this afternoon was confined to the 
periphery of this cloud shield along the areas that received 
more sunshine. Overnight tonight, there is still some 
indications of a weak circulation moving up the divide from the 
south which could result in continued stratiform rainfall. 
However, this moisture gets shunted further to the east by 
Thursday with a Rex Block forming to our west and the high 
pressure on top of the Rex Block introducing drier air across 
the west, keeping this moisture to our east. Storms will fire 
Thursday afternoon across the high terrain along this periphery,
so there is a chance that we see some heavier rates with 
thunderstorm activity. However, the instability and forcing is 
lacking so do not expect storms to last very long and be more of
the pop and drop variety while the southern divide might see 
continued stratiform rainfall. QPF numbers have come down even 
further with the latest model runs, probably due to the eastward
shift in the better moisture, less instability and lack of 
forcing. Decided to keep the Flood Watch going through Thursday 
night given the amount of rainfall received thus far across 
southwest San Juans and southern valleys, in case any area 
rivers see some rises in response and any convection could lead 
to heavier rates on already saturated soils. 

By Friday, the deepest moisture gets shunted eastward as the 
Rex Block breaks up and the low over the Baja weakens and lifts 
across the Desert Southwest and Four Corners as an open 
shortwave Friday afternoon. More sunshine Friday morning will 
result in more instability to fire scattered showers and storms.
The focus does seem to be across southwest Colorado where 
abundant rainfall has already fallen. This shortwave moves east 
by Friday evening, with drier air behind it and a high pressure 
ridge building in for the weekend. So we will see another break 
in the active weather this weekend. 

Looking ahead to early next week, the models are struggling 
with whether or not we will see remnants of Hurricane Polo get 
pulled into the region. While the weather does get more active 
with some moisture returning and scattered showers and storms, 
the latest model runs of the GFS and ECMWF are also bringing in 
a rather progressive low pressure trough into the Great Basin 
and across our region around the same time frame that Hurricane 
Polo moves inland across the Baja. So, some tropical moisture 
may get pulled northward but the deeper trough may keep the 
deeper moisture south of the Four Corners as another high 
pressure ridge tries to build across the west. GFS is trending 
drier while the EC is trending wetter. There's a lot that can 
change about the forecast between now and early next week, but 
this is a situation to keep an eye on over the coming days. 
Regardless of whether the moisture is tapped from Hurricane 
Polo, or just from more typical subtropical Pacific sources, the
return of showers and cloud cover will see temperatures drop 
below normal once more.
